title: Opening at two standard deviations
objectives: Open a trade when the spread diverges by two standard deviations.

screens.title: The first divergence
screens.prose: The spread of the first year's closest pair, A minus B, through its trading period. Its formation sd is 0.0210, so the dashed lines sit at ±0.0419.
screens.question: On which trading day does the spread first move beyond a dashed line?

hints.text: Follow the line from day 0.
It first leaves the band on the lower side.
Day 28 is the first day beyond −2 sd.

feedback.correct: Correct. Day 28 is the first open.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the first day the line is outside both dashed lines.

byKey.early: Day 10 is where it first passes 1.5 sd. The trigger here is 2 sd.
byKey.cross: Day 43 is where the spread crosses zero, which closes the trade.

explain.text: On day 28 the spread is -0.0532, beyond −0.0419 for the first time. Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst (2006) open a pair on that day. Every earlier day stays inside the band.

screens.title: Moving the trigger
screens.prose: Slide the trigger from 1.5 to 3 standard deviations. The caption counts how often the pair opens. Cointegration's "Entry and exit rules" used z-score thresholds; this is the same idea, measured in formation sds.

state.caption: Trigger 2 sd = 0.0419: the pair opens 4 times.

frames.caption: Trigger 1.5 sd = 0.0315: the pair opens 6 times.
Trigger 2 sd = 0.0419: the pair opens 4 times.
Trigger 2.5 sd = 0.0524: the pair opens 3 times.
Trigger 3 sd = 0.0629: the pair opens 2 times.

screens.question: At a 3 sd trigger, how many times does the pair open?

hints.text: Slide to 3.
Read the count in the caption.
At 3 sd it opens 2 times.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Slide to the last frame and read the count.

explain.text: The pair opens 6, 4, 3 and 2 times at 1.5, 2, 2.5 and 3 sd. A wider trigger means fewer trades, each from a larger gap. The paper fixes 2.

canvas.caption: Trigger 3 sd = 0.0629: the pair opens 2 times.

screens.title: Which leg is long?
screens.prose: On day 28 the normalised prices are A = 1.1715 and B = 1.2247. The spread A − B is negative. The trade bets on the gap closing.
screens.question: Which side does the desk take?

options.text: Buy A, the cheaper normalised price, and sell B

options.why: You bought the dearer share. That bets on the gap widening.

options.text: Sell both, as B is expensive
options.why: Selling both is a bet on the market falling, not on the gap.

hints.text: Which share must rise, relative to the other, for the gap to close?
A is below B in normalised terms.
Long the cheaper (A), short the dearer (B).

feedback.correct: Correct. Long the laggard, short the leader.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The cheaper share is the one to own.

byKey.longB: You went long the dearer share. That trade gains only if the gap widens.

explain.text: A sits below B, so A is the cheap leg. Long A and short B gains as the gap closes. This is the **opening rule**: beyond 2 sd, buy the cheaper and sell the dearer.

screens.title: How many units £1 buys
screens.prose: Each leg is £1. Prices are normalised, so £1 buys $1 / p$ units of a leg priced $p$. A is at 1.1715 on day 28.
screens.question: How many units of A does £1 buy?

hints.text: Units = money / price.
0.8536 units of A; B gives 0.8165.

feedback.correct: Correct. 0.8536 units of A and 0.8165 of B.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide £1 by A's price.

byKey.price: That is the price, not the units.
byKey.other: That is B's count. A is the long leg here.

explain.text: £1 buys 1 / 1.1715 = 0.8536 units of A, and the £1 short sells 0.8165 units of B. Equal pounds, unequal units. Each leg's gain is units times its price change.

screens.title: Three triggers on one pair
screens.prose: The same pair, three triggers. Use the explore screen's counts. The payoff is the sum over all round trips, before costs.
screens.question: Fill the number of opens for each trigger.

hints.text: A lower trigger is crossed more often.
1.5 sd opens on days 10, 25, 44, 59, 67 and 116.

feedback.correct: Correct. More opens at a lower trigger.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count each separate trip beyond the trigger.

explain.text: On this pair 1.5 sd earns most, 0.2718 from 6 trips. That is one pair in one cycle, not evidence for a lower trigger. Level 3 shows why choosing it on the same data overfits.

screens.title: A sign error
screens.prose: A backtest flips the sign: on day 28 it buys B and sells A. It closes on day 43, at the crossing. The correct trade earned 0.0574.
screens.question: What does the flipped trade earn?

widget.accept: -0.0574: the same moves with the signs reversed

hints.text: Each leg's gain becomes a loss.
Long B, short A is the mirror of long A, short B.
The payoff is −0.0574.

feedback.correct: Correct. The mirror trade loses what the right one gains.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Reverse both legs and the payoff changes sign.

byKey.same: You kept the correct trade's payoff. Buying the dearer leg turns convergence into a loss.

explain.text: Buying the dear leg bets on divergence, so convergence costs 0.0574. A sign error like this turns a profitable pairs book into a steady loser. A unit test on a toy pair catches it.

screens.title: Already beyond on day one
screens.prose: Edge case. A pair ends formation with its spread at 2.4 sd. On day 0 of trading it is still beyond 2 sd.
screens.question: What should the code do on day 0?

options.text: Open at once: day 0 is a trading day like any other
Wait for the spread to cross back inside and out again
options.why: The rule is a level, not a crossing. A spread beyond 2 sd on day 0 qualifies.

options.text: Skip the pair for this cycle
options.why: Nothing in the rule excludes it.

hints.text: Is the opening rule a level or a crossing?
It asks whether |spread| > 2 sd today.
Day 0 qualifies, so the pair opens on day 0.

feedback.correct: Correct. The loop must start checking on day 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The rule compares today's spread with 2 sd, nothing more.

byKey.wait: You treated the trigger as a crossing. It is a level test, met on day 0.

explain.text: The rule tests the level each day, so day 0 opens. Code that looks for a crossing from inside, or starts its loop on day 1, misses these trades. The tests on the next screen include one.

screens.title: Opening in code
screens.prose: Write three helpers. `first_open` returns `(day, side)` for the first day with |spread| > mult × sd, or `None`. Side is +1 when the spread is positive (short i, buy j) and −1 when negative. `units` returns the units £1 buys of each leg.
screens.question: Complete `threshold`, `first_open` and `units`.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np
def pairs_panel(seed=2006, n_ind=10, per_ind=10, n_pairs=20, days=3024, half_life=8.0, ou_sd=0.008,
                rw_sd=0.015, break_day=1512, break_frac=0.8, half_spread=0.005):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    N = n_ind * per_ind
    ind = np.repeat(np.arange(n_ind), per_ind)
    mkt = np.cumsum(0.0003 + 0.010 * rng.standard_normal(days))
    indf = np.cumsum(0.008 * rng.standard_normal((days, n_ind)), axis=0)
    phi = 0.5 ** (1.0 / half_life)
    u = np.cumsum(rw_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, N)), axis=0)        # unpaired: random walks
    common = np.cumsum(rw_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, n_pairs)), axis=0)
    eps = ou_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, 2 * n_pairs))
    a = np.zeros((days, 2 * n_pairs))
    for t in range(1, days):
        a[t] = phi * a[t - 1] + eps[t]                                   # mean-reverting gaps
    broken = rng.random(n_pairs) < break_frac
    drift = np.cumsum(rw_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, 2 * n_pairs)), axis=0)
    for k in range(n_pairs):
        for j in (2 * k, 2 * k + 1):
            x = common[:, k] + a[:, j]
            if broken[k]:                                                # the pair stops co-moving
                x = x + np.where(np.arange(days) >= break_day, drift[:, j] - drift[break_day, j], 0.0)
            u[:, j] = x
    pair_ind = np.repeat(np.arange(n_ind), 2)[:n_pairs]
    ind[:2 * n_pairs] = np.repeat(pair_ind, 2)                           # two planted pairs an industry
    logp = np.log(50.0) + mkt[:, None] + indf[:, ind] + u
    mid = np.exp(logp)
    bounce = np.where(rng.random((days, N)) < 0.5, 1 + half_spread, 1 - half_spread)
    close = mid * bounce                                                 # closes at bid or ask
    return close, mid, ind, broken


def normalise(P):
    P = np.asarray(P, dtype=float)
    return P / P[0]


def ssd_matrix(Pn):
    G = Pn.T @ Pn
    d = np.diag(G)
    return d[:, None] + d[None, :] - 2 * G


def top_pairs(Pn, k):
    D = ssd_matrix(Pn)
    i, j = np.triu_indices(D.shape[0], 1)
    order = np.argsort(D[i, j], kind="stable")[:k]
    return [(int(i[o]), int(j[o])) for o in order]

close, mid, ind, broken = pairs_panel()
widget.how: Submit runs 10 hidden tests: toy spreads, a day-0 open, no open, a zero sd, a seeded pair, the units. Loading NumPy takes a few seconds the first time.

hints.text: Loop over the days with `enumerate`.
Guard `sd > 0`, so a flat pair never opens.
Return `(t, 1 if s > 0 else -1)` at the first qualifying day.

feedback.correct: Correct. The opening rule is three small functions.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check from day 0, guard a zero sd, and return None when nothing opens.

explain.text: Pair (2, 3) gives (28, −1): open on day 28, long share 2 and short share 3. The `sd > 0` guard handles identical paths from level 1. The day-0 test checks the loop starts at 0.

screens.title: The opening rule
screens.prose:
With formation sd $\sigma$ and normalised prices $p_i, p_j$:
$$\text{open on day } t \text{ if } |p_{it} - p_{jt}| > 2\sigma, \quad \text{long the cheaper, } \tfrac{1}{p} \text{ units each side}$$
screens.question: A pair's formation sd is 0.025. Beyond what gap does it open?

hints.text: The trigger is 2 sd.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the sd by 2.

byKey.one: 0.025 is 1 sd. The paper waits for 2.

explain.text: The trigger is 2 × 0.025 = 0.05 either side. A spread of +0.06 shorts i and buys j; −0.06 does the reverse.

screens.title: From alert to order ticket
screens.prose: A live pairs desk gets an alert: shares K and L are 2.1 sd apart, and K is the cheaper. The desk trades £1m a side. K's price is £58.40.
screens.question: How many K shares does the buy order ticket ask for, to the nearest share?

hints.text: Shares = pounds / price.
17,123 shares.

feedback.correct: Correct. About 17,123 shares of K, and £1m of L sold short.

byKey.units: That is shares per pound. Multiply by £1,000,000.

explain.text: £1,000,000 / £58.40 = 17,123 shares. The short ticket sells £1m of L at its own price. Equal pounds on each side is the paper's rule, scaled up.

ideas: Open when the spread is beyond 2 formation sds; the rule is a level test, met even on day 0.
Buy the cheaper normalised price and sell the dearer; a sign error turns convergence into a loss.
£1 a side buys 1/p units of each leg, so the units differ when the prices differ.

formula.name: Opening rule
formula.note: Long the cheaper leg, short the dearer, £1 each.

summary.trap: Going long the dearer leg turns a convergence trade into a divergence bet.

explain.text: The trigger is 0.036 and the spread is 0.040, so the pair opens. A positive spread means i is dear, so short i and buy j.
